title: Remember you will die
hook: Stoics, monks and many others kept death in view in order to live better

segments.voice: Yesterday: Earthrise, the whole Earth with no lines on it. Your line was no borders from up there.

Old European paintings are full of them, once you start looking. A still life: grapes, a lute, a candle, a pocket watch. And, tucked among them, a human skull. Or a rich merchant's portrait in furs, with a skull on the table beside his hand. The painters weren't being morbid. The skull was a message, and it hung in homes, where it would be seen every day. After a week of looking at life from above, here's a closer look at the end of it. The message fits in two Latin words.
screen: `GRAPES, A LUTE, A CANDLE.` → `AND A SKULL.` → `TWO LATIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Memento mori: remember that you will die. More exactly, remember to die: remember that you are going to. It sounds grim. The people who practiced it said it did the opposite. The Stoics practiced it. Marcus Aurelius reminds himself, more than once, that he could leave life at any moment, and should let that shape every act and thought. Not fear: focus. If this could be the last conversation, you don't waste it sulking. In Christian monasteries, the Rule of Saint Benedict lists among its tools for good works keeping death daily before one's eyes. For the monks, this was bound up with hope in God and the life to come. The Hebrew Bible has its own version, in Psalm 90. In the King James words: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. Counting the days, not to be afraid, but to be wise. Buddhist texts teach mindfulness of death, maranasati, as a spur to live with care; the Buddha's own five remembrances come in a few days. These traditions mean very different things by death and what follows it, and i won't blend them. But they share one practical claim: remembering the end changes the middle. The petty argument looks petty. The phone call to your father looks urgent. An ordinary Tuesday looks like what it is: one of a limited number.
screen: `REMEMBER THAT YOU WILL DIE.` · `THE STOICS: NOT FEAR, FOCUS.` · `BENEDICT: DEATH DAILY BEFORE YOUR EYES.` · `NUMBER OUR DAYS.` · then, large: `THE END CHANGES THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Feel your breath going in and out, a thing that will one day stop, and don't push away any feeling that comes. Then, once, quietly inside: memento mori, remember you will die, and let it land softly. Ask what matters today, one person, one task, one kindness, and let the answer come while you just breathe, alive.
Memento mori. Latin for remember you will die, kept in view by Stoics, monks and many others in order to live better. Today's word.
Your line: one of a limited number. Remembering the end changes the middle. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Stoics, Christian monastics and Buddhist practitioners keep death in view on purpose: through daily reflection, the Rule of Benedict's instruction, the Psalms, or mindfulness of death, each within its own beliefs about what death means.

original.note: Latin: remember that you will die; more literally, remember to die.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: hook no longer opens 'Walk into'; cut 'one of the oldest practices there is' (superlative) and the doubled 'Today'; cut 'sixth century' (date not in the cited Rule chapter); 'made it a daily exercise' and claims about what buyers wanted softened; howItsDone 'many' to 'some'.
Meditations 2.11 and Rule of Benedict ch. 4 ('to keep death daily before one's eyes') are paraphrased; confirm.
AN 6.19 (Maranassati Sutta) cited for mindfulness of death: confirm the reference.

The trapdoor claim that the phrase 'memento mori' is medieval rather than classical: confirm (the Roman triumph story, 'respice post te, hominem te esse memento', is late and uncertain, and is deliberately not told).
Vanitas still lifes and portraits with skulls: mainly 16th–17th century Netherlands; confirm the hook's description.
